title: Establishment of a neoadjuvant organoid-based treatment for patients with gastric cancer
summary:
Treatment of Locally Advanced, Resectable Gastric Cancer

Gastric cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Although the overall incidence of gastric cancer has declined in many Western countries, cancers arising at the junction between the esophagus and the stomach have become increasingly common. Many patients are diagnosed only after the disease has reached an advanced stage.

Since the publication of the landmark MAGIC trial, perioperative chemotherapy (treatment given before and after surgery) has been the standard of care for patients with locally advanced but operable gastric cancer. Modern treatment regimens such as FLOT have further improved survival and cure rates. Nevertheless, many patients experience disease recurrence after initially successful treatment.

A particularly strong response to preoperative therapy is observed in approximately 30% of patients. This is defined by the presence of fewer than 10% viable tumor cells in the primary tumor after treatment. If the disease recurs, curative treatment is usually no longer possible, and therapy is primarily palliative, aiming to slow disease progression and relieve symptoms. The median survival of patients with metastatic gastric cancer is approximately 13 months. In patients whose tumors overexpress HER2, the addition of targeted therapies such as trastuzumab and, in some cases, immunotherapy can extend survival to approximately 16–20 months.

Personalized Treatment of Gastric Cancer

Under FLOT therapy, about one-third of patients achieve a favorable treatment response. However, this also means that roughly two-thirds derive limited benefit while still being exposed to the side effects associated with chemotherapy drugs such as docetaxel, 5-fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin.

The addition of modern immunotherapies to perioperative treatment has further reduced the risk of disease recurrence and improved outcomes. As a result, FLOT combined with an immune checkpoint inhibitor has become a new standard treatment approach. Nevertheless, only a subset of patients achieves a strong therapeutic response. To date, no established method exists to reliably tailor perioperative treatment to the individual biological characteristics of each patient's tumor.

Organoids as a Basis for Personalized Therapy

Organoids are an innovative cell-culture technology in which stem cells or tumor cells are grown outside the body to form small three-dimensional structures that closely resemble the original organ or tumor.

Researchers can now generate so-called patient-derived organoids (PDOs) directly from tumor tissue obtained from individual patients. Collections of these organoids have been assembled into biobanks, enabling large-scale testing of potential therapies.

Research groups, including the laboratory of Prof. Stange at the University Hospital Dresden, have established comprehensive gastric cancer organoid biobanks that capture the biological diversity of this disease. Results from the OPPOSITE study demonstrated that gastric cancer PDOs can be used to predict whether a tumor is likely to respond to FLOT therapy. In the future, this technology may help clinicians select the most effective treatment for individual patients while avoiding unnecessary side effects.

interventions.name: Patients with locally advanced adenocarcinoma of the stomach or the gastroesophageal junction who are candidates for neoadjuvant chemotherapy undergo, as part of the initial diagnostic workup in accordance with the S3 guideline “Diagnosis and Treatment of Adenocarcinomas of the Stomach and the Esoph

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Histologically confirmed, resectable adenocarcinoma of the gastroesophageal junction or the stomach (cT2–4, cNx, M0 or cTx, cN+, cM0)  
• Planned administration of neoadjuvant systemic therapy 
• No contraindications to resection of the primary tumor in the form of a 
subtotal/total or transhiatal extended gastrectomy or thoracoabdominal esophageal resection 
• Female and male patients ≥ 18 years of age 
• Patient is capable of giving informed consent. 
• Consent also given for future research projects within the framework of 
research collaborations with other university and non-university 
institutions
Exclusion criteria:
• Patients with distant metastases, including peritoneal carcinomatosis 
• Patients with recurrence (with or without prior incomplete or complete 
tumor resection) 
• Patients who have previously received systemic tumor-specific therapy (such as 
chemotherapy or targeted therapy) 
• Patients who, due to their general condition, are not expected to be eligible for surgery 
• A second malignant disease that occurred < 5 years ago (exception: early-stage localized tumor with in-sano resection, e.g., in situ carcinoma of the cervix, adequately treated basal cell carcinoma of the skin) 
• Patients who are housed in a closed facility
